title: What the diffusion coefficient means
question: What changes when D changes?
summary: D sets how fast a spreading cloud widens. Along one line, the mean square distance of its particles from where they started grows by 2D every second.

explanation.text: Put a drop of dye into a long tube of still water. At first the dye sits in one spot; an hour later it has spread along the tube, thinner and wider. The diffusion coefficient D says how fast that spreading goes.

The rule it follows is local. Look at one spot. If the dye is thicker on both sides than at the spot itself, a dip, dye drifts in from both sides and the spot fills. If the spot is a peak, thicker than its neighbours, dye drifts out and it thins. The more sharply the dip or peak is curved, the faster it changes, and D sets the pace. With p for how much dye sits per metre of tube at place x and time t:

explanation.spoken: The time rate of change of density is D times its spatial curvature.

explanation.text: The right-hand side is D times the curvature, which is positive at a dip and negative at a peak. For one particle instead of a drop of dye, p is the probability per metre of finding it at x. Where the tube ends matters too: a closed tube keeps all its dye, and after a long time spreads it evenly, not in the ever-widening bell of an endless tube.
The same rule can be read as a flow. The amount crossing a point each second runs from thick to thin, faster where the density falls more steeply:

explanation.spoken: Fick’s constitutive law sends flux down the density gradient.

explanation.text: Combining the flux law with conservation gives the diffusion equation for constant D. The flux law itself is a model premise in this route, not something conservation alone proves.

example.text: Suppose the dye's typical distance from where it started is 1 mm after one minute. Double D, keeping everything else the same: the mean square doubles, so the typical distance becomes about 1.4 mm, the square root of 2 times as far, not twice. Keep the original D and wait four minutes instead of one: the typical distance doubles, to 2 mm. Neither comparison says where any single particle goes.

exampleTitle: Doubling the diffusion coefficient, then quadrupling the time
stoppingPoint: D has units of length squared per time; boundary conditions and model premises must be stated.
